article.title: Why Model Monitoring Needs More Than Accuracy
article.why: 理解 label delay 下的 production monitoring，並結合 data quality、distribution、score 與業務 KPI。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Model monitoring in production needs more than accuracy because true labels often arrive late. A fraud model may not know which transactions were truly fraudulent for weeks. A churn model may need months before customer outcomes are confirmed. During that delay, accuracy cannot be measured in real time.

Teams therefore need several layers of monitoring. The first layer is data quality. Are required fields present? Did a numeric feature suddenly become zero for everyone? Did a category disappear because an upstream system changed? Missing values, schema changes, and impossible ranges can break a model before any accuracy metric moves.

The second layer is input distribution. If customer age, transaction amount, device mix, or another important feature shifts sharply, the model may be operating in a different environment from the one it learned. Distribution shift does not prove that performance is worse, but it is a useful warning signal.

The third layer is score distribution. Even when raw inputs look reasonable, predicted probabilities may move unexpectedly. A model that normally assigns high-risk scores to five percent of cases might suddenly assign them to forty percent. That can indicate a data problem, a population shift, or a real business event.

The fourth layer is operational behavior. Are predictions reaching downstream systems? Are decision rules using them correctly? Is latency increasing? A model can be statistically healthy while the surrounding pipeline is failing.

Business metrics provide another view. Approval rate, conversion, manual-review volume, complaint rate, or loss rate may change before labels are complete. These metrics are not perfect substitutes for model accuracy because many other factors affect them, but they can reveal that something important has changed.

Once labels arrive, teams can calculate the real performance metrics: AUC, precision, recall, calibration, profit, or other task-specific measures. At that point, earlier monitoring signals can be compared with the eventual outcome to learn which alerts were actually useful.

Good monitoring also needs thresholds and ownership. An alert without a response rule creates noise. Teams should define what change triggers investigation, who reviews it, what comparisons are made, and when retraining or rollback is considered.

Baselines matter too. Comparing today only with yesterday can miss slow drift. Monitoring should include recent windows, historical ranges, and important seasonal patterns. A holiday spike may be normal; the same spike in a quiet month may be suspicious.

The goal is not to detect every statistical difference. Large systems naturally change. The goal is to identify changes that threaten model validity, data integrity, or business operations.

Production monitoring is therefore a layered system. Accuracy remains essential, but it is often delayed. Data quality, feature distributions, score distributions, operational metrics, and business KPIs provide earlier signals. Together they help teams investigate problems before final labels arrive.

Teams should also monitor the relationship between features and predictions. A feature can keep the same average while its relationship with the target changes. Segment-level views are useful too: overall score distributions may appear stable even while one region, device type, or customer group changes sharply.

Alert design should avoid both silence and overload. Thresholds that are too loose miss meaningful problems; thresholds that are too sensitive create alert fatigue. A practical approach is to combine statistical thresholds with business impact. A small shift in a high-volume segment may matter more than a large shift in a tiny segment.

Documentation matters during incidents. When an alert fires, responders need to know the feature owner, source table, recent pipeline changes, model version, and expected seasonal behavior. Monitoring is most valuable when it shortens diagnosis, not when it merely produces charts.

Finally, teams should review monitoring rules after real incidents. If an outage was visible in missing-value rates but no alert existed, add one. If an alert fires every week without action, redesign it. Monitoring should evolve with the system.
paragraphs.zh: Production model monitoring 不能只靠 accuracy，因為真實 label 常延遲。應同時監控資料品質、輸入分布、score distribution、operational health 與業務 KPI，等 label 到齊後再回頭驗證哪些 early warning 真正有效。
